params.question: In compartment syndrome of the forearm, what property of the deep fascia makes the condition a surgical emergency?

answers.text: It is highly vascular and bleeds profusely when torn

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Deep fascia is relatively avascular. The emergency arises not from bleeding but from the inelastic nature of the fascial sleeve, which cannot expand to accommodate swelling.

answers.text: It is richly innervated, producing unbearable pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While compartment syndrome is painful, the surgical emergency results from the deep fascia's inability to stretch. Rising pressure compresses nerves and blood vessels, risking irreversible ischaemic damage to muscles and nerves.

answers.text: It is inelastic and cannot expand to accommodate swelling, compressing nerves and vessels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Deep fascia forms a rigid sleeve around each compartment. When a fracture or crush injury causes swelling, the fascia cannot stretch, so intracompartmental pressure rises and compresses the neurovascular structures — requiring emergency fasciotomy.

answers.text: It adheres to bone and prevents fracture reduction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Deep fascia does attach to bone via intermuscular septa, but this does not cause compartment syndrome. The emergency arises because the inelastic fascia traps swelling, raising pressure until nerves and blood vessels are compressed.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key property is that deep fascia is inelastic. When swelling from a fracture or crush injury fills a closed fascial compartment, the pressure rises because the fascia cannot expand. This compresses nerves and blood vessels, requiring emergency fasciotomy.

Exactly right. The deep fascia is inelastic — it cannot stretch. When swelling fills a closed fascial compartment, pressure rises and compresses nerves and vessels, making fasciotomy an emergency procedure.

interactions.label: A patient with a C5–C6 cervical disc prolapse reports numbness in one digit. Bas

params.question: A patient with a C5–C6 cervical disc prolapse reports numbness in one digit. Based on the autonomous zones of upper limb dermatomes, which digit is most likely affected?

answers.text: Index finger

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The index finger lies within C6 territory but is not its autonomous zone — it has significant overlap with adjacent dermatomes. The autonomous zone for C6, where overlap is minimal and testing is most reliable, is the tip of the thumb.

answers.text: Middle finger

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The middle finger tip is the autonomous zone for C7, not C6. A C5–C6 disc prolapse compresses the C6 nerve root, whose autonomous zone is the tip of the thumb.

answers.text: Thumb

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The autonomous zone for C6 is the tip of the thumb — the area with least dermatomal overlap. A C5–C6 disc prolapse compresses the C6 nerve root, making the thumb tip the most reliable site for detecting sensory loss. Remember: thumbs-up for C6.

answers.text: Little finger

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The little finger tip is the autonomous zone for C8, not C6. A C5–C6 disc prolapse affects the C6 root, whose autonomous zone is the thumb tip.

overallFeedback.feedback: A C5–C6 disc prolapse compresses the C6 nerve root. The autonomous zone for C6 — the spot with least dermatomal overlap and therefore the most reliable for testing — is the tip of the thumb. Remember: give a thumbs-up for C6.
Well done. The C6 autonomous zone is the thumb tip — remember the 'thumbs-up for C6' mnemonic. Since dermatomes overlap extensively, testing at the autonomous zone gives the most reliable result.

interactions.label: The ulna directly articulates with the proximal row of carpal bones at the wrist

params.question: The ulna directly articulates with the proximal row of carpal bones at the wrist joint.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is a common misconception. The ulna does not directly articulate with the carpal bones. The triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) lies between the ulnar head and the carpals. The wrist joint's proximal surface is formed by the distal end of the radius and this articular disc — not the ulna itself.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Despite being one of the two forearm bones, the ulna does not directly contact the carpal bones. The triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) — an articular disc — separates the ulnar head from the carpals. The proximal surface of the wrist joint is formed by the distal radius and this disc, articulating with the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetral.

params.question: On a lateral elbow radiograph of a child who fell on an outstretched hand, the anterior humeral line passes anterior to the capitulum instead of through its middle third. What does this finding most likely indicate?

answers.text: A normal anatomical variant in a growing child

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The anterior humeral line should pass through the middle third of the capitulum at any age. Failure to do so is an important radiological sign of bony displacement, not a normal variant.

answers.text: Posterior displacement of the distal humerus due to a supracondylar fracture

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: When the anterior humeral line misses the middle third of the capitulum, it indicates posterior displacement of the distal humeral fragment — the hallmark of an extension-type supracondylar fracture, the most common elbow fracture in children.

answers.text: Anterior dislocation of the radial head

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Radial head dislocation is assessed by the radiocapitellar line (a line through the radial shaft should bisect the capitulum in all views). The anterior humeral line specifically assesses the position of the distal humerus relative to the capitulum.

answers.text: Delayed ossification of the olecranon

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Delayed ossification would affect the visibility of the olecranon centre on the radiograph, not the position of the anterior humeral line. This displacement pattern indicates a supracondylar fracture.

overallFeedback.feedback: The anterior humeral line should pass through the middle third of the capitulum. When it misses — passing anterior to the capitulum — it indicates posterior displacement of the distal humerus, the hallmark of a supracondylar fracture, which is the commonest elbow fracture in children.

Correct. The anterior humeral line normally bisects the middle third of the capitulum. When it passes anterior to the capitulum, the distal fragment has shifted posteriorly — classic for an extension-type supracondylar fracture in children.

interactions.label: During Allen's test, both wrist arteries are compressed until the hand blanches,

params.question: During Allen's test, both wrist arteries are compressed until the hand blanches, then the ulnar artery alone is released. What does flushing of the palm within 5–7 seconds confirm?

answers.text: The radial artery is the dominant supply to the hand

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Allen's test specifically checks whether the ulnar artery can supply the hand on its own. Flushing after ulnar release confirms ulnar competence, not radial dominance.

answers.text: The ulnar artery provides adequate collateral supply through the palmar arches

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Allen's test confirms that the ulnar artery, via the palmar arches, can maintain adequate hand perfusion even if the radial artery is occluded. Flushing within 5–7 seconds means the collateral circulation is intact and radial artery cannulation is safe.

answers.text: The palmar arches are absent and the ulnar artery supplies the hand directly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Flushing actually confirms the palmar arches ARE functional, connecting the ulnar supply to the entire hand. Absent arches would mean poor collateral flow and an abnormal Allen's test result.

answers.text: The median nerve is intact and controlling vascular tone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Allen's test assesses arterial supply, not nerve function. The flushing is a sign of adequate blood flow from the ulnar artery through the palmar arches, confirming it is safe to cannulate the radial artery.

overallFeedback.feedback: Allen's test checks whether the ulnar artery provides adequate collateral supply to the hand via the palmar arches. Flushing within 5–7 seconds after releasing the ulnar artery confirms intact collateral circulation, making radial artery cannulation safe.

Exactly. Allen's test confirms that the ulnar artery can supply the hand adequately through the palmar arches. This ensures that cannulating or occluding the radial artery will not compromise hand perfusion.

interactions.label: A newborn presents with webbed fingers (syndactyly). Which embryological process

params.question: A newborn presents with webbed fingers (syndactyly). Which embryological process most likely failed during upper limb development?

answers.text: Proliferation driven by the apical ectodermal ridge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The AER drives proximal-to-distal growth via FGF signalling. Its failure causes limb truncation (e.g. amelia or phocomelia), not webbed fingers. Syndactyly results from failure of the process that separates the digit rays.

answers.text: Sonic Hedgehog signalling from the zone of polarising activity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Excess Sonic Hedgehog from the ZPA causes polydactyly (extra digits), not syndactyly (fused digits). The ZPA controls anterior–posterior patterning of the limb. Syndactyly specifically results from failure of interdigital apoptosis.

answers.text: Apoptosis of the interdigital mesenchyme

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: During week 7, programmed cell death (apoptosis) eliminates the tissue between the finger rays, sculpting individual digits from the hand plate. When this process fails, the digits remain connected — producing syndactyly.

answers.text: Lateral rotation of the limb bud in week 8

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lateral rotation positions the elbow posteriorly and the palm anteriorly. Its failure would affect limb orientation, not digit separation. Syndactyly specifically results from incomplete apoptosis between the finger rays during week 7.

overallFeedback.feedback: Syndactyly results from failure of apoptosis — the programmed cell death that normally separates the finger rays during week 7. Without this process, the interdigital mesenchyme persists and the digits remain webbed.

Correct. In week 7 of development, apoptosis separates the digit rays from the hand plate. Failure of this programmed cell death leaves the digits connected — syndactyly. Each step of limb development has its own named anomaly when it fails.
